content_metadata.description: This video tutorial demonstrates how to determine the modulus of elasticity for the material of a wire using Searle's apparatus. It describes the apparatus setup, the principles and formulas involved, and provides guidelines to ensure accurate measurements.

qAndA.answer: The speaker says that the diameter of the wire should be measured at different positions to check its uniformity throughout its length.
qAndA.question: Why should the diameter of the wire be measured at different positions?

qAndA.answer: One wire, called the reference wire, is unloaded, and the other wire, called the experimental wire is loaded. The extended length of the loaded wire is compared to the reference wire to calculate the extension.
qAndA.question: Why are two wires used in Searle's apparatus?

qAndA.answer: To minimize back lash error, the micrometer screw should be moved gently and slowly and in one direction only, ensuring the circular scale motion matches the linear motion.
qAndA.question: What precautions should be taken to minimize the back lash error?

qAndA.answer: The speaker mentions that as the experimental wire is elongated under a deforming force, its diameter does decrease slightly.
qAndA.question: Does the diameter of the wire change during the experiment?

qAndA.answer: The speaker advises that if a copper wire is used, due to its softness, the hanger assembly weights need to be adjusted carefully to ensure they do not exceed the elastic limit of copper and cause permanent deformation.
qAndA.question: If a copper wire is used as the experimental wire, what should one keep in mind?

narrativeProgression.description: The speaker introduces the topic of determining the modulus of elasticity for the material of a wire using Searle's apparatus.
The speaker defines elasticity as the property of a body to regain its original shape and size once the deforming force is removed.
The speaker explains that modulus measures the extent of elasticity for any material.
The speaker mentions Young's modulus of elasticity for the wire's material.

narrativeProgression.description: The speaker describes the components and functionality of Searle's apparatus, including its metal frames, spirit level, micrometer, and wire setup.
The speaker shows a diagram of Searle's apparatus and explains the terms experimental wire and reference wire.
The speaker presents the principle of Searle's apparatus based on Hooke's law and provides the formula for calculating Young's modulus of elasticity.

The speaker discusses the observations required for the experiment, including the length and diameter of the wire, least count of measuring instruments, zero error, acceleration due to gravity, and weights used.
The speaker presents a sample observation table with readings for diameter and micrometer measurements, explaining how to calculate the mean radius.

The speaker explains a sample observation table used to record data during the experiment, including loading and unloading readings of the micrometer and how to calculate the extension for a specific load.
The speaker summarizes the steps to analyze the collected data and calculate Young's modulus of elasticity using the formula and the SI units for each variable.
The speaker shows a sample calculation for Young's modulus using the formula and SI units.
The speaker suggests plotting a graph of load versus extension to determine Young's modulus and provides instructions for creating the graph and using its slope for calculation.
The speaker emphasizes plotting load on the x-axis and extension on the y-axis, resulting in a straight line graph whose slope can be used to accurately calculate Young's modulus.
The speaker provides the formula for calculating Young's modulus using the slope of the load-extension graph.
The speaker addresses various questions related to the experimental setup, starting with why Searle's apparatus uses two wires.
The speaker explains that two wires are used to compare the extended length of the loaded experimental wire with the unloaded reference wire.
The speaker explains why the two wires should be thin and long, emphasizing the need for measurable extensions under small deforming forces.
The speaker explains that using thin and long wires allows for significant strain to be produced by small deforming forces, making the extension easier to measure.
The speaker addresses the question of why both wires should be made of the same material.

The speaker highlights the importance of using the same material for both wires to minimize the influence of temperature changes on the experiment's accuracy, ensuring that only the load affects the extension.
The speaker explains why measuring the diameter of the experimental wire at different positions is necessary.
The speaker emphasizes that measuring the diameter at different positions helps to ensure that the wire is uniform throughout its length.
The speaker addresses whether the diameter of the experimental wire changes during the experiment.
The speaker acknowledges that the diameter of the experimental wire does decrease slightly due to elongation under the deforming force.
The speaker poses a question about whether reducing the length of the wires would change the value of Young's modulus (Y).

The speaker explains that Young's modulus is a material property and does not depend on the wire's length. However, using a shorter wire would result in very small extensions, making accurate measurement challenging.
The speaker discusses the role of the spirit level in the experiment and the reason for leveling it after each load adjustment.

The speaker clarifies that the spirit level is used to ensure both wires are of equal length at the start of the experiment and to measure the extension accurately after each load is added or removed.
The speaker explains why adjusting the spirit level should be done only after a sufficient time gap following each loading/unloading.
The speaker highlights the importance of allowing enough time for the wire to fully extend or contract after a load change to get an accurate measurement of the extension.
The speaker discusses which measured quantities have the most significant impact on the accuracy of determining Young's modulus.

The speaker points out that accurate measurement of the wire's diameter and extension is crucial because any errors in these measurements will significantly affect the calculated value of Young's modulus.
The speaker introduces the concept of backlash error and explains its relevance in the experiment.
The speaker describes backlash error as the play or lost motion between loosely fitting machine parts, specifically the micrometer screw in this experiment.
The speaker provides guidelines to minimize backlash error by moving the micrometer screw gently and slowly in one direction only.

Formula for Y using the slope
Text on screen: Why should we have two wires?
Explanation of two wires: We load one, and compare its extended length with the other unloaded wire.
Text on screen: Why should the two wires be thin and long?
Explanation: So that small deforming force produces significant strain
Text on screen: Why should the two wires be of the same material?
Explanation: Because the physical conditions like temperature has impact on the behavior of material and therefore keeping same material wire neutralise its effect
Text on screen: Why should we measure the diameter of the wire at different positions?
Explanation: To check its uniformity
Text on screen: Does the diameter of the experimental wire change during the experiment?
Answer: Yes , extension causes the wire to become thinner
Text on screen: Would the value of Y change if the length of the wires is reduced?

Answer: No, Y is the property of the material of which the wire is made. However, for shorter experimental wire the extension would be too small for the same load :stress remaining the same, Y remaining same, extension would be smaller to keep strain same
Text on screen: What is the role of spirit level in this experiment and why do we level it each time after we add/subtract the load in hanger?

Explanation: The leveling of sprit level at beginning make sure that the reference wire and experimental wire are of same length. After adding/subtracting loads the experimental wire elongates/contracts and due to this, the bubble of spirit level gets displaced from its centre position. To level again, we move the screw up/down and we measure the small change in the length of experimental wire
Text on screen: Why should we adjust the spirit level only after sufficient time gap following each loading/unloading?
Explanation: Loading causes elongation and to allow for full extension for a load sufficient time should be given
Text on screen: Which of the quantities measured in the experiment is likely to have maximum effect on the accuracy in determination of Y?
Answer: Diameter of the wire and extension
Text on screen: What is back lash error? Why should we keep it in mind?

Explanation: Back lash is play or lost motion between loosely fitting machine parts. The micrometer screw is loosely moving about its axis. While recording extension the screw should be moved gently and in one direction. The circular scale motion in a screw should match the linear motion to avoid back lash error

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: We are going to determine the modulus of elasticity for the material of a wire using Sir's apparatus.
The property of a body to regain its original shape and size once the deforming force is
removed is called elasticity.
The modulus measures the extent of elasticity for any material.
If the wire is made of a material, this elasticity modulus is called Young's modulus of elasticity.
Sir's apparatus, it consists of two metal frames P and Q hinged together such that they
can move relative to each other in vertical direction.
A spirit level is supported on a rigid cross bar frame which rests on the tip of a micro
meter at one end and on a knife edge on the other.
Screw can move vertically.
The frames are suspended by two identical long wire of the same material.
Wire on the side of the screw is called experimental wire and the other is called the reference
wire.
The frames are provided with hooks at the lower end from which weights are suspended.
This wire carries a constant weight to keep the wire straight and taut.
Slotted weights can be placed to apply force to the experimental wire.
Principle, it works on the principle of Hooke's law.
If delta L is the extension in the wire of length L and radius R due to force F equal
to M g, the Young's modulus of the material of the wire is Y is equal to M g into L divided
by pi R square delta L.
Let us analyze our observations.
Our observations for the diameter of the experimental wire, you must take at least three
readings at different locations and find the average or mean value.
Our observation table looks like this.
The first column has load on hanger in kilograms, micrometer reading loading in millimeters,
micrometer reading unloading in millimeters, you have a column for mean or average value
and you have the last column for extension for 2 kg load.
Let us see how we can analyze the observation and calculate the value for Y.
In the last column, we are going to put extension for 2 kilograms.
How are we going to do that is by choosing say 2.5 and 0.5.
So the reading for 2.5 minus that for 0.5 will give me the extension for 2 kilograms.
This value comes out to be 1.11.
Likewise with 3 and 1 kilogram, the difference will give me for 2 kilograms which will be
3.5 minus the reading for micrometer for 1.5 kilograms.
Again, will give me 2 kilogram and that will be 1.22.
Average that out and your reading is 1.18 millimeters.
You can put all the values in meters.
This calculation in SI unit after plugging the values in the formula will be giving us
m g l upon pi r square delta l and the result can be calculated as 7.31 into 10 is
part of 10 Newton meter square.
We can also find the value of Young's modulus using a graph.
So if you plot a graph of load and extension, keeping the load on the x axis and extension
on the y axis, you will get a straight line.
Within experimental error, the slope of the line can be found accurately and this can
be placed in the formula for y equal to l upon pi r square into 1 upon slope.
Now, why should we have 2 wires?
We load one and compare its extended length with the other unloaded wire.
Why should the 2 wires be thin and long?
So that small deforming force produces significant strain.
Why should the 2 wires be of the same material?
Because temperature can influence the material of the wire, the reference and the experimental
wire are subjected to the same changes in condition and therefore, it is only the
load which is responsible for its extension.
Why should we measure the diameter of the wire at different positions to check its
uniformity?
Is the value for diameter going to change during the experiment?
Yes it will because you are elongating the wire.
Under the deforming force, its diameter is bound to become lesser.
What the value of y change if we reduce the length of the wire?
No, it would not.
Why?
It is the material property.
However, you would get very small values of extension because the stress remains the same
deforming force by unit area.
The material has not changed so y will remain the same and in order to keep that constant,
the value for strain will be very much smaller.
So the extension would be difficult to measure.
What is the role of spirit level in this experiment?
And why do we have to keep leveling it?
The leveling of spirit level at the beginning make sure that the reference wire and the experimental
wire are of the same length.
After adding or subtracting load, the experimental wire elongates or contracts.
So you have to use the spirit level again and bring the bubble back to the center in order
to check out the extension.
Why should we adjust the spirit level only after sufficient time gap?
When you load the experimental wire, it takes some time to extend completely and we have
to allow for this time otherwise your reading would not be accurate.
Now which of the quantities in all your measurements is going to have the largest effect on your
calculation?
It is easy to understand that it would be the diameter of the wire because you are taking
r as a square and also the extension which is measured in millimeters by the micrometer.
Now what is backlash error?
And why should we keep it in mind?
Backlash is play or loss motion between loosely fitting machine parts.
The micrometer screw is loosely moving about its axis.
While recording extension, the screw should be moved gently, slowly and only in one direction.
The circular scale motion in a screw should match the linear motion to avoid backlash error.
So, we have learnt today how to measure the modulus of elasticity using a wire which meant
that we were looking only for Young's modulus of elasticity.
You can do similar experiment by changing the material of the wire.
You can choose copper wire though it is very very soft and your hanger assembly weight
should change in order to not to cross the elastic limit.
You can work it for stainless steel or steel wires, iron wires and a lot of other experiments
can be done to determine Young's modulus of elasticity for wires which are commonly
in use.
